The map's label, from 1279 to 1400, for two neighbouring mountain lands in the far north of South Asia: the Kashmir Valley and Ladakh, a high desert on the edge of Tibet.

Kashmir was ruled by Hindu kings of the Lohara line until the early 1300s. Their rule collapsed after a Mongol raid in 1320. A Buddhist prince from Ladakh, Rinchan, seized the throne and became a Muslim. In 1339 his former minister Shah Mir took power and founded the Shah Mir dynasty of the Sultanate of Kashmir. Persian scholars and Sufi preachers such as Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani came in these years, and Islam slowly became the faith of most of the valley.

Ladakh was a Buddhist kingdom ruled by a dynasty that traced itself to the old Tibetan Empire. Its people spoke a Tibetan language and its monasteries followed Tibetan Buddhism. It traded wool, salt and goods along routes linking Kashmir, Tibet and Central Asia.
